John Lamb

Bassist John Lamb was born in Vero Beach, Florida on December 4, 1933. His diverse path in life has included a stint in the Air Force, performing with Duke Ellington, teaching in public school, and a return to the jazz arena.
John was interviewed in Clearwater Beach, Florida on March 16, 2001, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and we are in Clearwater Beach and I’m very pleased to have bassist John Lamb with me here today.
Thank you.
And I’ve been looking forward to talking to you for a couple of weeks now. You’ve kind of come full circle. You were born down here, weren’t you?
I was born in Vero Beach. Yes. I wasn’t too proud of it at the time but—
Why is that?

Well it was a small town and nothing, as far as I was concerned, and it was in the middle of nowhere. Although it was like, I’m sure it was a small paradise because it was right there on the east coast where all the beautiful beaches were. But the attitudes were in a different direction at that time and that’s why I didn’t want to be from Vero Beach.
Can you tell me about those attitudes?

Those attitudes I discovered one day on television when I was in my twenties. So the television told me, it said hey, this is what happened to you when you were growing up in Vero Beach, or growing up in Fort Pierce, which was 15 or 16 miles a way, south of Vero Beach. But anyway I was born on a farm in Vero Beach. My mother used to work, used to be a domestic. And we played along with all kids, everybody had a great time, I grew up thinking that I was well adjusted and a fine young man, I felt good about myself you know and everything. And then later on, I would say I moved where I had to go to St. Augustine at age a year and a half or two, and then my father died at age, what about three, three and a half. Then I had, among relatives, all kinds of relatives, and they moved me back to Ft. Pierce. My mother was in Vero Beach and she used to come by once a week to see me and I lived there with them because they could better take care of me. And so I grew up in Ft. Pierce, another area that I stayed in until graduating from high school at age 16. I didn’t realize it was a big deal at the time but most people graduated at 18. I didn’t realize it but during that time you could graduate at age 16 and there was nothing else to do but study.
There was no distractions. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

No distractions, right, sure. But I wasn’t proud of the area, like I said, because of the attitudes among the people. I grew up feeling good, like I said, about myself. But I discovered one day watching the tube that there were different things going on as compared to other parts of the country as far as the working relationships, the social aspect of it, the equal rights so to speak part of it. Those are the things that I didn’t feel good about later on.
You found out that you had grown up in an area that —
That wasn’t too cool.
—that wasn’t too cool.
That’s right, sure. But I mean I felt good about it. I mean at the time, as a kid, if you’re born in a situation and you don’t know any differently, then it’s okay, sure.
And your friends were white and black.

Yes. Sure. My employers were white, and I felt good about them. They were very nice to me. But there were other things that were out there that maybe I was unaware of at that time. My teachers were excellent. I loved my teachers so much that I wanted to become a teacher. And I felt that they did a very good job with what materials they had, and the way they worked, sure.
After graduation, you had a career decision?

Yeah I had to earn some money. So I went to the man that was raising me at the time, my uncle, and I said, “what would you do now that you’re graduated from—” now that I’m graduated from high school. He says, “I’d go in the Army.” You know at that time it was an option. And I found myself walking Eighth Street in Ft. Pierce and everything was beginning to become a little bit boring. So I said well it’s time to do something different. So I went into the Air Force. I went down to Miami, I stayed 2 or 3 days for the induction part of it, and I had to wait. Actually I was 16 when I really applied. I had to wait until I was 17. And then when I turned 17, in December, they said okay, we’ll induct you now with your mother’s permission. So my mother signed me into the Air Force. Down while being in Miami, I ran into those social things. Because here we are in one building being tested for the military, and then we had a break for lunch and they says, “okay, everybody hop over across the street and get lunch.” So I walked with the rest of the cats across the street to get lunch. I walked in there and everybody looked up at me as if I was from a different planet or something. And so I ignored it, and they ushered me back to the kitchen while my buddies ate. So it was sort of a time when nothing could be done about that.
This was about 1950?
Oh, it was December of ’50, exactly. So I had my lunch and went back to the post office and continued to enroll into the military. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
And when you got in the military—

Okay they put us on a train see? They put us on a train and you went out to — you know during those days blacks and whites had to ride in separate cars. But one thing I noticed on this particular coach, they put us all in the same coach. I said this is different, we are riding in the same coach. So anyway we went up through Alabama. We got to Alabama, it’s time for another lunch break, right? So they says, “you have to get off the train and go across the street and get something to eat.” So I walked right into the place there, and one of the guys says, “we can’t serve that guy over there.” And they says, “John, would you like me to bring you a sandwich or something?” So then we go out, and I says, “all right, that’ll be fine.” So back on the train, and we hopped on towards San Antonio. That’s where the inductees were brought at that time. So two little incidents right there.
And were you in uniform at that time?
Not at that time, no. Not at that time. So we went through the training and all of that. And by the way, I was a tuba player.
Oh, okay. Now we have to backtrack and we’ll talk about the music, but this is very interesting.

Okay, well I played the tuba and there was a warrant officer in there that heard me play, and my tone was very good, and I could play the chromatic scale and the B flat major scale and my reading was down a little bit. And he says, “your reading is not good but you have a very good tone.” He says, “I’ll give you six months to come up to par.” So he gave me a break. His name was Proctor. Warrant Officer Proctor. Proctor used to be with the band in Lockburn, at Lockburn I believe. There was an all-black outfit and he eventually became a Warrant Officer and I just happened to run across him at this time and he gave me a break. Now after that little bit of training in San Antonio they moved us up to Montana.
Oh boy.
Great Falls, Montana. Could you imagine being there?
From Florida. Whoa.

So I hopped off the thing, the what do you call it, the train, and all this snow, and I’d never seen snow before. I was definitely curious. So they shuffled us on out to the air base. But after having been there at the air base for a while I began to become more involved in the music. They gave me six months, like I said, to come up to par, which I did, and sort of surpassed a few others that were there that had been there a few years that had become complacent you know. Then one day the first sergeant says, “we have a man on leave here, John, do you play bass?” I said, “sure, I play bass, no problem.” So I went over and pretended that I—
You didn’t play bass. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

No I didn’t really play bass. And he says, “yeah, go ahead and try it.” His name was Earl Evans. He was a tech sergeant. He was somewhere, what’s that, Nebraska or someplace now. And he says, “go ahead, try it.” So I picked it up. He says, “you want to try it for a few days? I says, “yeah.” So I took it up and I learned how to tune G D A and E, and because of my tuba experience I would play root and fifth, I learned what root and fifth were, the finger here and the finger there you know, that type of thing. So I did that for about two or three days, and I was good enough to play the gig that Friday night, playing my root and fifth, and like two-beat, that type of thing. And of course time made it a little better. And I began to make some kind of progress somewhere, and they offered me like a ten dollar job at the service club, or the NCO club or something like that. And they gave me my ten dollars, and I says this is pretty good. And the old bass player came back off leave in 30 days and they wanted me instead of him. Why? Because of my ability to feel the music and to feel the swing of it. And so this continued on, and I continued to practice. And then one day we had a group come in from out of town that played a little jazz for us. They didn’t have a bass player. So I sat in with them and they encouraged me. And I later found out that they were living in Great Falls, that they were from in town. So they encouraged me to come in, so I did. I went in and took a bass there and sat in with them. But I later discovered that the place was off limits. So I had to sneak into the club and when the policemen came in I would have to get on the bandstand and play. And so I did that for a long time, maybe a couple of years, getting all this experience.
Did you have to be in uniform when you’d go into town like that?
No.
Okay. Because otherwise you’d be like — you’d really stick out in there.
They could tell by my shoes, they looked at my shoes. Everybody wore black shoes in the Air Force you know.
Interesting. What would the, can you recall, at one of those very first gigs you played as a bass player, what were some of the songs that you would have played at the time?
You mean with that Air Force group?
Yeah.
Let’s see. We were into Stan Kenton.
No kidding?
Yeah, I heard a lot of Kenton at that time because the guys would bring their records. And I didn’t listen to jazz or anything like that. I remember “Apple Honey.” [scats] Was that Woody Herman’s?
Yeah. “Autumn —”
Yeah, Autumn something. [scats] The saxophones. It was a saxophone thing. And I learned the parts to that by learning to read the parts. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
Okay. So you had some music.
Yeah.
All right.

And then I listened to a lot of people in town there and the influences were, I heard guys bring in recordings of Stitt & Ammons, I heard a recording of Fats Navarro. I heard a lot of Kenton and a lot of big bands. And then I heard this bass player called Safranski. Ed Safranski. And what I did I said hey that’s pretty good, everybody seems to like it. Because he would feature certain people in certain sections. And so I learned Safranski’s bass part and that taught me some scales. I had to dig for some positions. They weren’t necessarily correct positions, but I learned the scales from having played tuba. And I went to town to see if I could find a book and I did find a book, and it was Bobby Haggart’s book. He had pictures on there. Later on down here I told him about that. And I think he got a kick out of it. He said that was the best book that was ever written for bass, that was his saying. But anyway Bobby Haggart had some influence there through his method. And then some people would come through town, I remember a guy’s name was Gene, that’s all I remember, blonde, had a beard, had a space in the front, and I went over to his hotel room and I wanted to get a lesson or two. “What do you want to know?” I didn’t know what I wanted to know, I just wanted, you know. And that was it. So little experiences like that. But up there in Montana I got the chance to work with some of the musicians there and there was one fellow by the name of Rudy Williams, he played sax, tenor. He says, “you know what? You sound like my cousin.” I said, “who’s your cousin? He says, “Charles Mingus.” I had never heard of Mingus you know. That’s what he said. And what was I to know? I’m just a kid that’s playing a bass. And then one night on the jukebox, while playing in the same joint, I heard something coming out of the box, a trio. I didn’t really know what the combination was, but it was something. I said to one of the guys in the band, I said, “who is that playing bass?” And he said, “that’s Ray Brown.” I said hmmm, so I began to edge closer to the jukebox. And I listened to this and I said it sounds good, a nice tone and it sounds almost like a tuba. And then Oscar Peterson was on piano and Herb Ellis I believe or either Barney—
Barney Kessel.
Yeah Barney Kessel. Later in life I worked with both of those guys.
That’s great.

And then I met Ray and Oscar and all those, we did gigs together. Well anyway I began to investigate Ray Brown, like when I went on leave I heard some of his things coming out of a jukebox in Savannah, the trio playing. And I said that’s Oscar, huh? And then I began to investigate Charlie Parker and I used to listen to that because guys would bring © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
their music in and I’d listen and listen and listen. I don’t know if I was really learning anything but it was part of my consciousness now.
Wow. What was your actual job in the service?
My job was a tuba player.
So you got through the service as a tuba player?
As a tuba player, yes.
You played for the marches.
Yes, everything.
You played the sousaphone also?

Yeah, sousaphone, yeah. And I did that for about, that hitch for about three years. And I learned a lot from other musicians and the method books and observing what they were doing and so on. But I’ll tell you another experience I had one day in the latrine. We had to go through Basic again because we hadn’t completed Basic in Texas. So we had to go through that again. And one day I was in the latrine practicing the tuba. So one of the guys, a staff sergeant walks in and says, “you think you’re so damn smart, what are you practicing for?” Well I’m trying to figure out where does this come from? “What are you practicing so much for?” And I was just practicing and practicing. It turns out that I think he was very drunk, he had been drinking and when he got to that stage he went a little bit crazy. I later on met him too and I confronted him with that in Vero Beach.
In Vero Beach.

Yeah. But I did it in such a nice way, the man had changed completely, he was a different person. He had had some problems in his childhood that reflected in his daily living so I understand that. No problem. But anyway this experience lasted for about three years, this military experience. And I became — got out. But just before getting out I met a fellow by the name of Oscar Tunnard. Oscar was supposed to be one of these brainy guys that could remember everything. He played that way. He was from St. Petersburg originally. And what is he doing up in Montana? But anyway I met him in Montana. And he used to talk about a place called the Schillinger House. It’s the old — well it’s Berklee now. It’s Berklee School of Music. And it used to be the Schillinger House because Schillinger used to, that’s where—
The Schillinger Method.

Quincy Jones went there. But anyway he talked about that and he says if he had his choices he would go to Berklee, or to Schillinger House. So somehow that stayed in my head. I said well I think I’ll go up and try it. And so after we were discharged and working with this monster pianist for six months I decided to give that a shot. But prior to leaving the military again, I was talking to this piano player Oscar about Ray Brown. I says, “you know this Ray Brown guy?” And of course we’d been listening to Shearing © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

and all that and Oscar, those were the two major pianists at the time. He says, “yeah, I’ve heard of Ray Brown.” And he says, “there’s a guy down in Miami can do everything Ray can do.” I says, “who is that?” He says, “Sam Jones.” I didn’t know who Sam Jones was. I’d never heard of him. And later on he was working with Cannonball and quite a few others. And I met him later on in my career, yeah. Anyway I get out of the military and decide that I’d try to go back to Vero Beach. I went to Vero Beach and got a job at a packing house, you know, to make some money. And there wasn’t anything going on there. I mean everything was domestic, I tried cleaning and I wondered if I could work in a hospital as an orderly or something. And it didn’t turn out too well. I think I stayed in the packing house a little over a week or two weeks, and I had $27 saved up. I didn’t even get along with my parents, my mother at that time, because I had changed. You know when you’re in your early twenties it’s very difficult to get along with parents at that age, because I knew quite a bit. She says, “well what you should do, John,” she says, “is take this job until you can find something else.” But there was nothing else better in Vero Beach. Have you been to Vero Beach?
No.
Well it’s a lot different today.
I think so.

But it had about 16,000 people at the time. And it was a very small town. So I decided to take my $27, I said, “well I’m going to Boston to Schillinger House.” I didn’t have any money or anything like that. So I said, “I’m heading for Schillinger House.” So I hopped on the bus—
Is that right?

Yeah, I hopped on the bus, moved on up, and I think it was two or three days to New York. When we got there for a break the porter outside says, “where are you going?” I says, “I’m going to Boston.” He says, “what do you do?” “I’m a musician.” He said, “what are you going up there for? Everything is right here.” He says, “you’ll be back.”
This is in New York?

Yeah. We’re taking a little break there, yeah. Yeah, “you’ll be back.” I said, “okay,” so I hopped on and went to Boston. Because I knew I had met somebody that was originally from Vero Beach by the name of Henderson and he says, “well come on up we’ll help you out.” So I went up there and I found out he was a Pullman porter. So they put me up in the Pullman porter’s place for, what, seven dollars a week. So he gave me a room and I tried to wait tables. I remember the first job I ever tried to do up there and the guy says, “you’ve got to have a tux.” I had a black suit, double breasted. It looked good, a nice, black suit. I went on and he gave me a table and all that, and he gave me a tray. I had never done this stuff. And he said, “this is your table, by the way, is that a tux you have © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

on? That’s not a tux. Out.” So I was out. So anyway I ended up getting a job at Steuben’s Restaurant in Boston as a dishwasher. And I washed a few pots and pans. And I think that lasted a little over a week too. But in the meantime I went back to the Schillinger House and asked for my application fee back. I think it was like $25 or something.
You asked for it back?

Yeah. He says, “we don’t normally do this.” Probably the dean. But he says, “we understand your situation.” This is where Herb Pomeroy and all those people taught, and John LaPorta and all, they teach up there. And he says, “we don’t normally do this but we understand your situation” so they gave me the money back. And I took the money and applied it toward my room.
Did you decide not to go there because you just couldn’t afford it?

Well I couldn’t go there, no money. But while I was getting my money back, I heard this beautiful bass sound coming out of the room. Somebody was bowing this instrument. I said oh that’s so beautiful, I didn’t realize that a bass could sound like that. And all of this sound was filtering out. I don’t have any idea to this day who that was. But it stayed with me. And while washing these dishes, these pots, there was a group out in the lobby playing. And I looked out there and the guys all had tuxes you know, looking good. And of course I had a little musical background and I said that’s what I’d like to do, you know, play out there in the lounge. I shouldn’t be back here in washing these pots. So it turns out it was Joe Bruno’s father that was playing in that group. And Joe Bruno I met 20 years later, or much later, down in Sarasota. And I also met his son, so I met the father when I was in the kitchen, but not formally but through his music. And then I met the son later on down in Sarasota, and then his other son, his son, who plays bass. So we have three Brunos. But anyway after that little experience I got a job playing in another club, in Eddie Levine’s place on the corner of Mass and Columbus in Boston. And they said hmmm, they gave me an audition and all that. So I played my Ed Safranski solo.
All right.
They had a little quartet you know, I mean that’s all I knew. And I’d walk a little time, and I had my Chubby Jackson model five string bass.
Oh you did. I’ll be darned. That’s right he had his own little.

Yeah, he had this five string bass. But you know later on I discovered that Slam Stewart tuned his bass with a high C on top. And I didn’t realize that at the time. And then in that little corner we had the Hi-Hat, we had all the jazz cats come over there. Are you familiar with Boston? Mass Columbus? We had that little corner, we had Wally’s across the street where I met Pops Foster. Pops Foster was 75 about that time and he was claimed to be the first guy to begin plucking the bass. And I said, “Pops, come on over, I want you to catch my act and see how I do on the bass.” So he came out and checked out my sound © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

and he says, “good sound.” And you know, encouragement. And in this little joint, Eddie Levine’s, I met all kinds of musicians, they used to come up and visit our leader, who was Dean Earl. And as far as my style and being a gentleman and being in the business and all that, was a fellow by the name of, like I said, his name was Dean Earl. And he talked about good manners and musicianship and personality, being on and off the stand, and not drinking excessively. He says, “if you’re going to drink, always have a good meal first.” You know, that type of thing. And so he was like a mentor. And so Dean was also a graduate of Berklee. He also taught there and all those things. And he advised me as far as schools are concerned. He says, “if I were you,” he says, “I would go to a different school.” He says, “Berklee doesn’t offer you a teaching degree.” So I thought about it, so I went over to the New England Conservatory and I hang around the practice room a little bit, just getting the feel of things and all that. And in the meantime at the Hi-Hat across the street, I used to hear all of these groups come in, all these small groups. Guys like Shadow Wilson and Miles Davis and Ella Fitzgerald and Hot Lips Page, and all those kind of people. And then there was another place called The Shell Bone, not The Shell Bone, there was a famous club in New Orleans at one time, there was another club in Boston, George Wein—
Oh yes, Storyville.

Storyville. George Wein owned that. And the big man in town was Jimmy Woode, the bass player, and Junior Raglin, whenever Duke would come to town would come by and sit and play. And I’d listen to these guys and I’m beginning to pick up on what they — I says now what’s so appealing about that? I says I can do that. And so on. And got a chance to hear Basie over at Storyville and I heard Duke and I heard Charlie Parker and Prez along with Duke’s band, and the singers, Joe Williams, and that thing “Every Day” that they put out.
“Every Day I Have the Blues.”
Yes. I used to go up to the jukebox late at night and listen to that all the time, listen to that bass player, Ed Jones. Remember Ed Jones?
Yeah.

And I listened to that kind of things. And in the meantime I had a gig after hours right across the street there, what was it called, I don’t know but anyway it was a little after- hours joint. We played from maybe two to five in the morning. You know, I mean that type of thing. And one night Billie Holiday walks in. And she sits down on the side there with her little dog, a Chihuahua I think it was. And so put my hand out like this, and the dog grabbed me. She says, “honey don’t do that,” she says, “always do like this.” You know like put your hand out like that. She says, “he won’t bite you then.” She kept her little dog in her purse. And she sang one or two tunes with us that night. Just an informal © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

thing. It was during the Boston years. And the Boston thing just went on for a while and then my night gig ran out after a year. But I was making $50 a week. And all the other guys says, “well that’s a poor paying club” they says, “the guy didn’t pay you too much money.” But to me—
Fifty bucks.
Was fifty dollars. And I know I ate a lot of sardines and I ate a lot of, what do they call those things, peanuts and Coke. I ate a lot of those.
To fill you up.
And I would sleep late in the afternoon so I wouldn’t use up so much energy. That type of thing.
Man, you were paying some dues I guess.

I think I lost about, at that time I lost about ten or fifteen pounds. Of course today that would be great. But anyway that went on for a while and then I says I have to do something about this. I says it’s time for me to make a change. Because I’ve heard other people talking about that they needed a trade, and they were tired of going from one gig to the other and so on. But during this time in Boston, I got one good gig, I think I had a week with Ella. She was coming through Boston, or was in Boston already and they needed a bass player for Philadelphia. So I went down to the station with my bass. I was supposed to meet them. And I looked around and I didn’t see anybody, no Ella, no anybody. You know I’m just a kid, nobody. And so I says well maybe I should just hop on the train and I’ll see them at the next station or somewhere. So what I did, I don’t know why I did this, but I put my bass in the baggage room and left it there and I stayed on the train and sure enough there they were, waiting at the platform looking for me. “I wonder where the kid is.” There was Marcus Foss, the drummer who called me Junior, that type of thing. And Don Abney who was the piano player, and all these guys were well seasoned. And so Ella says, “oh there he is,” she says, “where’s your bass honey?” I said it’s at the station and then I tried to explain it and I couldn’t explain it. So that upset her quite a bit. And she says, “honey, always keep your bass with you.” She says, “Ray always took his bass with him wherever he went.” Because she used to be married to Ray. And so we hopped on the train to go to Philly. But my mentor, Dean, told me he says, “always keep a diamond on your finger, so whenever you have a problem you’ll be able to eat anyway.”
So you could pawn it?

So I had a little diamond ring that I had bought, because I was following my mentor see? Which was excellent advice. So I went to the music store and they had an old bass in the corner and I says, “well look man,” I said, “I’m working down here at Pep’s, and all I have is my ring, can I use your bass for a couple of days?” So he looked at the ring, he © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

says, “yeah, okay.” So he loaned me this bass, he asked me who was I working with. I told him Ella Fitzgerald, that type of thing, and so I took the bass and went down and worked with her a few days. Then in the meantime we sent for my other bass. And so it arrived, my Chubby Jackson model. And so I took it back. That’s how that happened, one week with Ella.
Yeah I bet the bass from the pawn shop didn’t have five strings on it.
Well actually no. It didn’t. Actually it wasn’t a pawn shop, it was a music store.
Oh, okay.
All the musicians used to go in there. As a matter of fact I bought my Ray Brown method book from there. Sure.
So you entered into your Philadelphia kind of time from there is that right?

Yeah. Well no, that’s another story. That’s another story. A week in Philadelphia and then I went to Atlantic City for a while, and then there was no more work. I says now what’s happening. I began to assess myself and I said well what’s happening. I says you do have a skill, you can play the tuba, you had a military career, well three or four years anyway, and I says you’re young and all those kinds of things. I says it’s time for you to do something. I hit rock bottom there as far as employment goes. And I’d see all these prosperous looking people and I says there’s nothing out here that I know how to do. What can I do? But there for a short time I did get a job in a haberdashery for about six months. And that had me going for a while. I substituted for a saxophone player. So between those two gigs, working a little bit at nights and the haberdashery, I was able to make it. But after that everything was — you know, because I had to live from day to day. So I decided, I says well I think I’ll go back into the Air Force. So finally that was my decision. I went back in the Air Force and I went back in this time with one stripe. Before I had no stripes. But I had one stripe. I went into the band, the guys had heard that I had worked a week with Ella or had worked with a few musicians around Boston you know, and I had a little prestige there.
You came with a reputation.

Yeah, and had a little tuba experience because I had done that before. So I was a little bit ahead of the game. But I said I have to really do something about my abilities. I says, I decided right there and then that I was going to become the world’s greatest bass player. I decided, that’s what I put into my head. I says you have to do it. I don’t know why, I think I was sort of like driven and I had experienced hunger, and I experienced the disappointments and all those kind of things. And I had a craving or a love, and then all these social things that I experienced before were coming through. You know what I mean? From what I experienced as a child. I didn’t know what they were, but I had to express all of this in some way, otherwise it would have come out in the form of pimples © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

you know what I mean? Anyway, I went back in the Air Force and I did this thing, and within six months I had an awakening. I mean really. I hit a low one day and then I had to go through these changes. I don’t know, it’s mental, physical, and it’s like an awareness came over me. I began to investigate spirituality a little bit. Psychology. All the books that I could read on the subjects that were on the base library I began to investigate. And I got rid of all my jazz records. And I had a whole slew of, I just tossed all of that aside. And while this was happening, going through this change, one of the guys came into the barracks one day and says, “John,” he says, “I found you a bass teacher.” As if like, you know, he just came out of nowhere. The guy used to play with the Cleveland Orchestra. His name was Tad Shetler. He played with them for about, well quite a number of years, over ten years, had to be. And he was also a pianist, a concert pianist. And after we got to meet each other I found out that he couldn’t get a job playing concert piano so he went to bass. And he had studied with the premier, the first chair of Boston. So in a sense I had gotten my teacher indirectly through him. And Mr. Shetler, I stayed with him for a couple of years, two or three years and learned what I could. Talk about — an awful sound I got out of the instrument, it was terrible. That Kay bass, it was terrible. Scratchy — didn’t know anything about bows or anything. And he taught me out of the Simandl Book, Franz Simandl. That’s the so-called bass Bible. And we worked with that and I scratched my way through it for about two or three years. And then somebody came up to me and said, “John, you want to go overseas? There’s an opening in Iceland.”
Oh jeez.
I says, “yeah, sign me up.” I wanted to get out of Roswell, New Mexico. That’s where we were. We were in Roswell, New Mexico.
Man I’ll tell you, you’ve been to some of the hot spots.

Oh definitely. That’s where they have the UFO sightings or something. And by the way in Roswell I had some experiences too, like social things. Like they had a sign up on the wall that says, “we refuse the right to serve anyone.” I mean I was a GI, you know, off base there trying to have a little fun with my buddies and that was on the wall. Did that attitude also include your fellow military people?

If it did I didn’t notice it too much. I don’t know why I didn’t pay too much attention, it was just something I just didn’t notice. I guess I was lucky that way. Not unless I had a direct confrontation. If I had a direct confrontation then I would sort of listen to it and ignore it somehow. I don’t know why but it just went on. It came out in the music I guess. Because now that you ask that question I did have an experience with a guy that I went on leave with once. He was a bagpipe player up in Montana. and he was from Tennessee. And he said, “do you know what a nigger is?” That type of thing. And I just sort of dismissed it. Boom. Gone. That’s the only direct thing that I can recall during that time. So instead I chose Shreveport, Louisiana, which was just as bad. So I went to Shreveport and everybody was fine on base. The problem was off-base because the city ordinances, yeah. And I had another thing that happened there, while I was in this spirituality thing. But anyway he would come out to the base, and he was a captain and I was a little, whatever it was, two or three stripes. And he’s walk in the barracks and everybody would snap to. And we’d talk about spiritual things. And he did that for as long as I was there at the air base.
And when you were in Louisiana, what year was this?

I think ’58, ’59, ’58. But on the air base everything was fine. There were quite a few officers that played instruments that had love for the music. And because I had my little prestige thing going they all wanted to come over and play with me. So we had that kind of relationship. There was no segregation as far as officers and enlisted men. And every time one of these guys would walk into the barracks or they came to see me, guys would snap up, and they said oh, John, meet so-and-so and let’s make this gig. You know what I mean? And that was the end of that. And while were we in Shreveport, like I said, this guy used to come out once a week and talk to me. After that, during that period they had a general conference of all the spiritual people getting together in this big auditorium in town. And I was a part of the group. “John, we’d like to have you come but there’s nothing we can do to get around this law.” So they says, “we have a solution. You comply with the law, you sit up there in the balcony,” and there were about five or six other people out there in the main auditorium there, and of course I was used to balconies, you know the movie theatres and that type of thing. So I was used to balconies. And so I put on my uniform, full dress you know, because I wanted to have this experience just to see. So I went through that experience and here was the representative to the main office talking to this spiritual group. Yeah, no distractions, right?

Then I might go to the movies for a couple of hours at 6 ‘til about 7:30 or 8, then come back and practice for a couple of hours until about 10 o’clock at night, and then go to the barracks at night, then start the process over the next day. And that’s the way that happened. And Great Falls — did I say Great Falls — Newfoundland was no different. They had social problems up there. They had private clubs. And unless you were a member of the club you couldn’t get in. And you know, no members were black members. So it was sort of like a subtle thing. But one on one, one on one I found that 99 or 98 percent of the people that I’ve met have always been nice people. It’s just that the laws were in such a state that it influenced thinking. And some people had grown up with the mentality that they were in some ways superior because, in some ways. But I knew differently. I still know differently. There is no such thing, it’s just an individual matter, it’s just who you are as a person. And maybe that’s always what I sense about individuals, and somehow whenever they said or did something that was disturbing, somehow it would just sort of go away. It didn’t bother me. I don’t know why.

Well as a kid I’d heard that the blues and rhythm was the devil’s music. And I didn’t really listen to the blues that much. I heard it, because it was a part of the scene. Getting back to that high school thing, I remember hearing Louis Jordan swing on the jukebox, singing “Caldonia” and all those things, and I’d see them in movies and I heard Tommy Dorsey’s [scats] and he’d play that long trombone solo on it, which was very nice. And I loved those things. They were all based on the blues. And of course the church was in there too, I used to go to church all the time and I’d hear them sing. And I knew that there was a difference between the church and the school, it didn’t seem real. It seemed to me like church was unrealistic as compared to what I experienced everyday in school. It seems like some kind of pie in the sky thing. Because he always preached the same sermons and it was always hell and — what do you call it? Hell and brimstone or something.
Fire and brimstone, yeah.

You know unless you come up and give me your hand and do such a thing, he says, you’re going to die and go to hell in a minute. So and what about that? My buddies, speaking about that hell and brimstone thing, my buddies you know, we were all about nine or ten years old. They were a little bit older than I was. So I saw them go up and get the preacher’s hand one day. And they says well it’s very nice that these young men have joined the church. So I didn’t want to be outdone by my buddies so I went up there and gave the preacher my hand. And he asked me some questions and I turned my head and whispered, the low part of my voice, and he would translate to the audience and, “well that’s very fine.” So we were all baptized and I was with my buddies again. And that’s how that part of it started, that church thing. And that’s all there was to do.
Well tell me about, in Philadelphia you had some of your own band-leading experiences, didn’t you? Did you lead some of your own groups eventually?

Well I led a group in the Air Force as well. And I had a trio around Philadelphia and I worked with Jimmy Heath and Specs Wright and Sam Dochre and Kenny Barron. Did I tell you I met Kenny Barron? I saw a bass player going into the subway one day. And I says, “hey, where are you going?” He says, “I’m going to a session.” I says, “you mind if I follow you?” So he says, “no, come on.” So I followed him around and he went over this guy’s house, the guy was playing piano. And I met a lot of musicians that were on the corner that played. I met Ray Gullin in Boston and worked with him for six months. I met the chief arranger for the Air Force band in DC, we worked together for a while. And now these were all very, very, very talented people, very smart and very hard working people. And there was something about them, some qualities about them that I liked. © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

They had those abilities to do these things. But I discovered that it was more work than just being smart. It was a lot of work. A lot of work. Effort. And a lot of things that I didn’t necessarily want to hear, like I said, musically. I had to go through all of that in order to reach the type of sound that I wanted to reach.

But later on I discovered that it was like a cousin to jazz you know. And I also discovered that there were some very fine musicians involved in country music. And when I hear them in person I get more out of a kick watching them in person than I do listening. And then the lyrics are so simple and so down to earth and so basic that in a lot of cases they’re worth listening to.
So, when did you decide that again you needed to exit from the Air Force?

Yeah. Great.
Yeah. It’s amazing. She is the one that encouraged the musical thing. She says, “you might be sorry someday if you don’t do that.” And it took a lot on her part to do that.
Yeah, sure. Especially when you start doing road work.

Well the rock & roll scene came along, but I also owned an electric bass. And it turned out to be — this was with Lionel Hampton’s band.
Oh, right.

pulled it out. Like the horse shows, the ice shows, that type of thing. Because you have to read. It’s like reading a book. You’ve done those shows, right?

Talk about trial by fire.

Yeah. Interesting. This was 1964?
Yeah, ’64, right. 1964.

I’m sorry, $60 a night?

Yeah probably $60 a job or something like that. And the stars were getting all the money. And my being, not knowing anything about charges and all that, and prices, I was just happy to get a gig. Yeah. And you were responsible for your own, putting yourself up?
Yeah.
The whole thing.

Yeah, I was responsible for that. But I began to pull my way up a little bit gradually financially. And my wife, being the type of person that she is, utilized the monies in a very positive way. I had heard something about that.
Yeah.

That’s right.

Well he would listen and he would put all of this together in composition. He’d listen. Anybody said something, he’d just let it go you know. And he’d walk around and he’d tell each person, this is the way it is. Then he’d go back to his regular self.
What kind of things would he say?
Well I can’t mention that on camera, you don’t say that kind of stuff. But he would use some words that were not too pleasant.
So every once in a while he had to kind of —

Yeah, he had to straighten everybody out. But most of the time he was just easy going. If he found somebody not pulling their end of the bargain he would feature them a lot. Like Paul used to go to sleep on the stand a lot. He’d always pull Paul out and feature him two or three times in a row.
That’s one way to keep them awake.
Right.

Yes. Sure.
He had his first gig with Duke.
He’s from South Africa isn’t he?

Yeah. And there was a guy by the name of Wolf Freeman who was from South Africa, a bass player. He used to come in, he had to come in by way of Canada and then to the United States. And I used to see him out there at Basin Street all the time.

Well not really. They were just substitutes. Short term players. It’s in this book here. He kept the same people, he had the same saxophone section the whole time I was there.
Right.
I’m sure you are familiar with all of those players.
Sure. © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-

Right. There was no rhythm guitar.
No.

No not all the time, no. I had to create a line to that, or if they didn’t have the music I had to draw from things I had heard years ago, like the old standards. Were the veterans in that band, did you have to like prove yourself to them, in their attitude towards you? You were always the newcomer?

Well to some degree. But I was kind of cocky. I knew what I was doing. And what they had to say didn’t matter. One, the one in L.A., we were playing at Disneyland and a riot broke out that night and they wouldn’t let us back to our places. We couldn’t get back there. Isn’t that amazing? Mercer made the announcement. “They says we can’t stay in town tonight fellas, we’ll have to stay on the outskirts.” And once in Milwaukee we went in with an armed guard I believe, they escorted us through the thing there.
